t: Maximum Number of Groups Entering a Competition
o: Partition all n students into groups 1..g where group sizes strictly increase (1, 2, ..., g at minimum) — grade sums can always be arranged to increase afterwards by putting large grades in later groups (any assignment works since we control membership; formally, sorting grades and filling smallest groups first guarantees increasing sums). Hence the answer depends only on n: the largest g with 1+2+…+g = g(g+1)/2 ≤ n. Example 1: n=6 → g=3 (6 ≤ 6). Example 2: n=2 → g=1 since 1+2=3 > 2.
k: Grade values are irrelevant — only the count n matters, because sizes must grow at least as 1,2,…,g and sums can always be made to follow suit.
Answer = max g with g(g+1)/2 ≤ n, obtainable by incremental counting, binary search, or the quadratic formula.
Sorting is unnecessary despite appearing in the tags.

a.i: Keep adding the next group (size grows by 1) while the cumulative triangle number stays within n.
s: g = 0, used = 0; while used + g + 1 ≤ n: g++, used += g.
a.t: O(√n) — g grows until g²/2 ≈ n.

a.i: Solve g(g+1)/2 ≤ n directly: g = ⌊(√(8n+1) − 1)/2⌋, using integer sqrt to dodge floating-point edge cases.
a.t: O(1) — one square root (plus safety adjustments).

w: Mention why grades don't matter: sort ascending and fill groups of size 1,2,… left to right — each later group has more, hence larger-or-adjustable sums (swap elements to fix any inversion). Pitfalls: trying to actually construct groups, and floating-point sqrt precision near perfect triangles (the adjustment loops fix it). Follow-up: minimize the number of groups, or constrained group sizes.
